Gastroenterology · published research

Intestinal injury (ischemia-reperfusion)

Summary of the Evidence

Five animal publications are relevant. One directly measured intestinal injury after ischemia-reperfusion and found no bowel protection at the tested protocol. Four related publications from a Brazilian research program examined remote lung inflammation or oxidative injury after gut ischemia-reperfusion. Those distant-organ findings should not be counted as evidence of intestinal healing (de Lima et al. 2011; Kirkby et al. 2012; de Lima et al. 2013a; de Lima et al. 2013b; de Lima et al. 2014).

Human and clinical evidence

No human PBM study for acute intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury was identified. The evidence comes from surgical rat and mouse models with early bowel or remote-lung measurements.

Animal evidence

The direct study assigned 96 male rats to 15 groups. After 60 minutes of superior mesenteric artery occlusion, a 650-nm, 70-mW laser delivered 0.5 J/cm² to the jejunal serosa immediately before or after reperfusion. Intestinal injury was worse with laser at 0 and 1 hour than with untreated ischemia-reperfusion and was not improved at six hours. Lung injury was lower in treated groups, indicating a distant-organ effect without bowel protection at this setting (Kirkby et al. 2012).

Four related publications used 660-nm light over the chest after intestinal or gut ischemia-reperfusion. Rat experiments reported lower lung edema, neutrophil influx, myeloperoxidase activity, tumor-necrosis-factor expression, oxidative stress, or airway reactivity and increased anti-inflammatory measures. A mouse dose-response study also reported lower lung inflammatory markers at several tested fluences (de Lima et al. 2011; de Lima et al. 2013a; de Lima et al. 2013b; de Lima et al. 2014). These studies support a remote-lung signal but do not replicate intestinal protection.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct bowel study used 650 nm at 70 mW and 0.5 J/cm² on exposed jejunal serosa immediately before or after reperfusion. The remote-lung studies used 660 nm over the upper bronchus or chest, with reported fluences from 1 to 7.5 J/cm² and treatment after mesenteric occlusion or reperfusion. These application sites and outcomes are not interchangeable, and operative serosal exposure is not equivalent to external abdominal treatment.

Interpretation

At the tested direct-bowel protocol, PBM did not protect the intestine and worsened early histology. Related experiments consistently report favorable remote-lung outcomes, but they address a different organ and largely come from one research program. With no human evidence, certainty remains very low for both intestinal protection and remote-lung benefit.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Very low for intestinal protection in acute rat ischemia-reperfusion injuryVery low for reduced remote lung injury in the same model

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One direct rat study found worse early intestinal histology and no bowel benefit by six hours, despite less lung injury. Four additional rat or mouse publications from one Brazilian research program reported favorable remote-lung outcomes after gut ischemia-reperfusion but did not test intestinal healing. No human study exists, so certainty remains very low for both intestinal protection and remote-lung benefit.
